title: Alaska Senate race: state and federal investigations into a 'spoiler' candidate days before the vote
dek: A New York Times report says Democrat Mary Peltola's campaign helped recruit a candidate who shares Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan's name. Alaska's governor and federal prosecutors have opened investigations; Peltola says she knew nothing about it.
happened: On 28 October The New York Times reported that Mary Peltola's campaign and aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee helped recruit candidates to split the vote of Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, including a candidate with a nearly identical name. Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy directed the state Department of Public Safety to investigate whether state law was broken. On 30 October Alaska's U.S. attorney, Michael Heyman, confirmed a federal criminal investigation; grand jury subpoenas had been issued after the report.

sides.says: "I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent," she said in Juneau on 29 October, calling the report "just another distraction". Her campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee denied recruiting candidates.

Trump called for Peltola and the namesake candidate to be removed from the ballot and prosecuted, calling it "Voter Fraud at the Highest Level". Vice President JD Vance backed an investigation. Gov. Dunleavy said the Times reporting "substantially supports" earlier findings by the state elections board.
Michael Heyman called the situation "deeply troubling" and said his office was acting "intensely and swiftly". He said no specific crime had yet been determined.

A former senior Peltola campaign staffer told the Times that Peltola was aware of the effort but not directly involved; the staffer later sought to withdraw those statements, and the Times said other evidence supported its reporting.

next: Alaska votes on 3 November. State courts found the namesake candidate qualified, so he stays on the ballot without a party label; the senator is listed as the Republican and the incumbent. The Times noted that recruiting candidates to split an opponent's vote is generally legal and has been used by both parties in Alaska.
summary: The dispute centres on Alaska's Senate race between Democrat Mary Peltola and Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, which could help decide control of the U.S. Senate. A New York Times investigation published on 28 October reported that her campaign and national Democratic aides helped bring other candidates into the race, including one with almost the same name as the senator. In the primary, Peltola received 48%, Sen. Sullivan 43% and the namesake candidate 2%. Gov. Mike Dunleavy ordered a state investigation, the U.S. attorney in Alaska confirmed a federal criminal inquiry, and President Trump called for prosecutions. Peltola denies any knowledge. Separately, the Trump administration has filed a civil lawsuit seeking to stop Alaska from certifying the result if Sen. Sullivan narrowly loses.
